title: Arrays Archipelago
description: Big O, arrays and hash maps: the tools behind half of all interview questions.

challenges.explanation: The inner loop runs n times for each of the n outer iterations, so the body runs n × n times.
n is halved every iteration, so it takes about log₂(n) halvings to reach 1.

challenges.prompt: Two loops, one after the other. What is the time complexity?
challenges.explanation: Sequential loops add: n + n = 2n, and constants drop, so it is O(n). Only nested loops multiply.
The outer loop runs n times and the inner loop doubles j until it reaches n, which takes log n steps. n × log n.

challenges.prompt: On average, how long does it take to check whether a key exists in a hash map?
challenges.explanation: A hash map jumps straight to a bucket using the key's hash, so lookups are constant time on average. Heavy collisions can degrade it to O(n) in the worst case.

challenges.prompt: Given an unsorted array and a target, return the indices of two numbers that add up to the target. Which approach gives O(n) time?
options: Sort, then binary search each element
Check every pair with two nested loops
One pass with a hash map of values seen so far
challenges.explanation: For each number x, check whether target − x is already in the map. One pass, O(n) time, O(n) space. Sorting would lose the original indices and costs O(n log n).

challenges.prompt: Build Two Sum using a hash map. Tap the lines in order.
challenges.explanation: Check for the complement before storing the current value, so a number is never paired with itself. Sorting would scramble the indices you need to return.

challenges.prompt: Group a list of words so that anagrams (like "eat", "tea", "ate") end up together. What is the cleanest approach?
options: Hash map keyed by each word's sorted letters
challenges.explanation: Anagrams share the same sorted letters ("aet"), so that makes a perfect hash key. Each word goes straight into its group.

challenges.prompt: You check whether an array contains a duplicate by adding each element to a set and stopping if it is already there. Time complexity?
challenges.explanation: Each element gets one O(1) average set lookup and insert, so n elements cost O(n). The trade-off is O(n) extra memory.
